Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Hammer: The claw hammer's split back came from nail-pulling needs, and the design has barely changed in centuries.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Chisel: A chisel shaves wood with a sharp bevel, and a good one can pare away paper-thin curls.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Hand saw: Western hand saws cut on the push, while Japanese saws cut on the pull, which allows thinner, finer blades.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Tape measure: A tape measure's tip hook is loose on purpose, sliding by its own thickness so inside and outside measurements both read true.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Level: A spirit level uses an air bubble in liquid, and the idea dates to the 1600s and is attributed to Melchisédech Thévenot.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Mallet: A wooden mallet strikes a chisel without mushrooming its handle the way a steel hammer would.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Plane: A hand plane shaves wood flat and smooth, and the curls it makes are called shavings.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Nail set: A nail set drives a nail head slightly below the surface, so the hole can be filled and hidden.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Square: A carpenter's square checks right angles, and the 3-4-5 triangle trick has been used since ancient times.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Clamp: A clamp is a carpenter's extra pair of hands, holding glued joints tight while they dry.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Wood file: A wood file shapes edges and curves that a plane can't reach.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Sandpaper: Sandpaper was reportedly made in 13th-century China using crushed shells glued to parchment.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Stethoscope: A stethoscope was invented by René Laennec in 1816, partly out of shyness, and he first used a rolled-up paper tube.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Whisk: A whisk belongs in the kitchen, where it whips air into eggs or cream.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Scalpel: A scalpel is a surgeon's blade, and its edge is sharper than most household knives.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Ladle: A ladle is a soup server, and has been in kitchens since the Bronze Age.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Stapler: A stapler belongs to the office, and the first staplers for paper came about in the 1800s.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Spatula: A spatula is a kitchen tool for flipping food, and the word comes from Latin for a flat blade.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Trowel: A trowel belongs to masons and gardeners, and the pointed mason's version is for spreading mortar.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Plunger: A plunger is a plumber's tool, and the rubber cup was patented by John Hawley in 1874.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Tongs: Tongs are used for gripping hot items, in a forge or a kitchen.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Sickle: A sickle is a harvesting tool, and crescent blades like it go back about 10,000 years.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Abacus: The abacus is an ancient counting frame, and it's still used for arithmetic in parts of Asia.
Tools in a carpenter's toolbox.Thermometer: A thermometer measures temperature, and Fahrenheit made the first mercury version around 1714.

Scientists who study living things.Biologist: The word comes from Greek bios, life. Biology only became a unified field around 1800, when Lamarck and others popularised the term.
Scientists who study living things.Zoologist: Zoologists cover every animal from sponges to blue whales, and many spend years watching one species just to decode its behaviour.
Scientists who study living things.Botanist: Botanists have named roughly 350,000 plant species, and new ones are still found every year, often in tropical forests.
Scientists who study living things.Ornithologist: Ornithologists study birds, and bird ringing, where a tiny band is put on a leg, has revealed migrations spanning whole continents.
Scientists who study living things.Entomologist: Entomologists have the biggest job in zoology: insects make up well over half of all known animal species.
Scientists who study living things.Herpetologist: Herpetologists study reptiles and amphibians, a pairing that looks odd, but the two groups were historically lumped together.
Scientists who study living things.Ichthyologist: Ichthyologists study fish, the most diverse group of vertebrates, with over 30,000 known species and more discovered yearly.
Scientists who study living things.Microbiologist: Microbiologists study life too small to see unaided, such as bacteria, and the human body holds about as many microbes as human cells.
Scientists who study living things.Mycologist: Mycologists study fungi, which are closer kin to animals than to plants; one honey fungus in Oregon spans several square miles.
Scientists who study living things.Marine biologist: They study ocean life, from plankton to whales, and the deep sea remains so unexplored that new species turn up on most expeditions.
Scientists who study living things.Geologist: Geologists study rocks and Earth's structure, not living things, though fossils make their work overlap with biology.
Scientists who study living things.Seismologist: Seismologists study earthquakes and the waves they send through Earth, which is how we know the planet has a liquid outer core.
Scientists who study living things.Meteorologist: Meteorologists study weather and the atmosphere, so they work with air and clouds, not living organisms.
Scientists who study living things.Volcanologist: Volcanologists study volcanoes, and some collect gas samples at crater rims; the field is physical science, not biology.
Scientists who study living things.Etymologist: Trap: this sounds like entomologist but is a different thing. Etymologists study word origins, while entomologists study insects.
Scientists who study living things.Cosmologist: Cosmologists study the origin and fate of the universe as a whole, which makes them physical scientists, not life scientists.
Scientists who study living things.Astronomer: Astronomers study stars, planets and galaxies. Astrobiology looks for life, but astronomers themselves mostly study non-living things.
Scientists who study living things.Physicist: Physicists study matter, energy and forces. Biophysics links the two fields, but physics itself is not a life science.
Scientists who study living things.Chemist: Chemists study substances and reactions. Biochemistry sits close to biology, but a plain chemist works mostly with non-living matter.
Scientists who study living things.Mathematician: Mathematicians work with abstract structures, not organisms, though their equations model how populations and epidemics grow.
Scientists who study living things.Mineralogist: Mineralogists study minerals, which are non-living crystalline solids. Some, like pearls and shells, are made by living things.
Scientists who study living things.Glaciologist: Glaciologists study ice and glaciers, and ice cores they drill hold air bubbles from hundreds of thousands of years ago.
Scientists who study living things.Linguist: Linguists study language, and they work on people and their speech, but they are social scientists, not life scientists.
Scientists who study living things.Numismatist: Numismatists study coins and currency. Another trap from the sound of the name: it has nothing to do with numbers or life science.

Jobs in a hotel.Concierge: The concierge, from a French word for keeper of the candles, arranges tickets, tours and tables, and a good one knows the city's secrets.
Jobs in a hotel.Bellhop: Receptionists are the first face at check-in, and they handle bookings, keys and a thousand small problems at the front desk.
Jobs in a hotel.Receptionist: The housekeeper keeps rooms clean and stocked, and a head housekeeper often manages dozens of staff and every linen cupboard in the building.
Jobs in a hotel.Housekeeper: Bellhops carry bags and show guests to rooms. They get their name from the bell once rung at the front desk to summon them.
Jobs in a hotel.Doorman: The doorman greets guests, hails taxis and can be the hotel's best source of local knowledge and gossip.
Jobs in a hotel.Night manager: The night manager runs the hotel from late to early, handling emergencies and late arrivals while most guests sleep.
Jobs in a hotel.Valet: Valets park guests' cars and bring them back on request. The word comes from the French for a male servant.
Jobs in a hotel.Chambermaid: Chambermaids clean and tidy guest rooms. The old word chamber means bedroom, which is where the job gets its name.
Jobs in a hotel.Porter: Porters carry luggage, a job as old as travel itself, and the word comes from the Latin portare, to carry.
Jobs in a hotel.Room service waiter: Room service waiters deliver whole meals to guests' doors, and the metal dome on the tray is there to keep food hot along long corridors.
Jobs in a hotel.Usher: Ushers guide people to seats at theatres and events, so a hotel does not usually have one on staff.
Jobs in a hotel.Golf caddie: Caddies carry golf clubs. Some resorts offer them, but a typical hotel has no such staff for its rooms and lobby.
Jobs in a hotel.Bank teller: A bank teller handles cash, and sometimes a hotel sits next door, but the teller is employed by the bank, not the hotel.
Jobs in a hotel.Midwife: Midwives deliver babies. Hotels are not hospitals, so this is one job you rarely find in a hotel lobby.
Jobs in a hotel.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks cut down trees in forests. They'd have little use in a hotel, apart from the timber for the building itself.
Jobs in a hotel.Shepherd: Shepherds look after sheep on hills and pastures, among the oldest jobs on earth, and are far from hotel lobbies.
Jobs in a hotel.Astronaut: Astronauts fly in space. A few have stayed in hotels, of course, but only as guests before a launch.
Jobs in a hotel.Coal miner: Coal miners work deep underground, and their job is one of the toughest and most dangerous in the world, nothing like a hotel's work.
Jobs in a hotel.Dentist: Dentists look after teeth. Some hotels have a doctor on call, but they rarely employ one on the payroll.
Jobs in a hotel.Umpire: Umpires keep order in sports like baseball and tennis, so this job belongs in a stadium, not in a hotel.
Jobs in a hotel.Jockey: Jockeys ride horses in races, and need to be tiny and fit. Nothing about hotel work calls for a racing silk.
Jobs in a hotel.Ship's captain: A ship's captain commands a vessel at sea. A cruise ship is a floating hotel, but its captain isn't a hotel employee in the usual sense.
Jobs in a hotel.Farrier: A farrier shoes horses, a craft that dates back over two thousand years. Few hotels have a forge on site.
Jobs in a hotel.Tollbooth worker: Tollbooth workers collect fees on roads and bridges. They work in a booth by a highway, not at a hotel front desk.

Characters with a well-known job.Bob the Builder: Bob the Builder's catchphrase is Can we fix it? Yes we can, and Neil Morrissey voiced him in the British version.
Characters with a well-known job.Fireman Sam: Fireman Sam works in the Welsh village of Pontypandy, and the original was created in Wales in 1987.
Characters with a well-known job.Postman Pat: Postman Pat has delivered the post in Greendale since 1981, along with his black and white cat Jess.
Characters with a well-known job.Mary Poppins: A nanny is her job, and in P. L. Travers's books she arrived on the east wind, and left when the wind changed.
Characters with a well-known job.Homer Simpson: Homer works as a safety inspector at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, a job he's famously bad at.
Characters with a well-known job.Fred Flintstone: Fred works at the Slate Rock and Gravel Company, operating a dinosaur crane, and says Yabba Dabba Doo.
Characters with a well-known job.SpongeBob: SpongeBob is a fry cook at the Krusty Krab, and in the show he has failed his boating test dozens of times.
Characters with a well-known job.Super Mario: Mario was a carpenter when he first appeared in Donkey Kong in 1981, then became a plumber.
Characters with a well-known job.Tintin: Tintin is a young reporter, and Hergé's Belgian comics about him have sold over 200 million copies.
Characters with a well-known job.Clark Kent: Clark Kent is a mild-mannered newspaper reporter at the Daily Planet, who is also Superman.
Characters with a well-known job.Peter Parker: Peter Parker works as a freelance photographer for the Daily Bugle, whose editor J. Jonah Jameson hates Spider-Man.
Characters with a well-known job.Willy Wonka: Willy Wonka is a chocolatier, and Roald Dahl's book was first published in 1964.
Characters with a well-known job.Winnie the Pooh: Pooh Bear has no job, and the original bear was named after a real Canadian bear, Winnipeg, at London Zoo.
Characters with a well-known job.Garfield: Garfield is a lasagna-loving cat who has no job, and Jim Davis created him in 1978.
Characters with a well-known job.Peter Pan: Peter Pan is a boy who won't grow up, and has no job, from J. M. Barrie's 1904 play.
Characters with a well-known job.Pikachu: Pikachu is a Pokemon with no job, and its name combines Japanese sounds for sparkle and a mouse squeak.
Characters with a well-known job.Bart Simpson: Bart is a schoolboy, not a worker, and his name is an anagram of brat.
Characters with a well-known job.Charlie Brown: Charlie Brown is a kid with a baseball team that never wins, who has no job.
Characters with a well-known job.Tweety: Tweety is a canary who has no job, and was originally pink because the first cartoon version looked naked.
Characters with a well-known job.Nemo: Nemo is a clownfish, who has no job, and nemo is Latin for no one.
Characters with a well-known job.Bambi: Bambi is a deer who has no job, and Felix Salten's 1923 book was originally written in German.
Characters with a well-known job.Dory: Dory is a blue tang fish with short-term memory loss, and has no job.
Characters with a well-known job.Tinky Winky: Tinky Winky is a purple Teletubby with no job, and has a bag on his arm.
Characters with a well-known job.Sonic: Sonic is a speedy hedgehog, who has no job, made by Sega in 1991 to rival Mario.

Things a mime uses at work.Invisible box: Mimes make walls look solid by freezing the hands at exactly the same spot, so the audience's brain fills in the surface.
Things a mime uses at work.White face paint: The pale face descends from Pierrot, the sad clown of French theatre, and keeps expressions readable from the back row.
Things a mime uses at work.Striped shirt: The black-and-white striped top is tied to French street performance, and its pattern makes arm movements easier to follow.
Things a mime uses at work.Beret: Though linked with France, the beret is Basque in origin and is worn by soldiers and artists around the world.
Things a mime uses at work.White gloves: White gloves make the hands stand out against dark clothes, so finger gestures show clearly from the back of a theatre.
Things a mime uses at work.Imaginary rope: A tug-of-war with an invisible rope is a mime classic; the performer sells it by leaning and straining against nothing.
Things a mime uses at work.Suspenders: Suspenders, called braces in Britain, finish the traditional street-mime outfit alongside the striped top.
Things a mime uses at work.Gestures: Mime tells stories entirely through body, face and hands, and the art goes back to ancient Greek and Roman theatre.
Things a mime uses at work.Silence: Silence is the rule, not a limit: by staying wordless, a mime can perform anywhere in the world without translation.
Things a mime uses at work.Microphone: A mime's act is silent, so a microphone would be pointless; the wordlessness is the entire art.
Things a mime uses at work.Megaphone: Megaphones amplify the voice, and a mime never speaks, so the performer has nothing to project.
Things a mime uses at work.Loudspeaker: Loudspeakers broadcast sound, which a silent act doesn't need, though music may play from one in the background.
Things a mime uses at work.Whistle: A mime stays silent, so even a whistle breaks the rule of the act; a referee needs one far more.
Things a mime uses at work.Karaoke machine: Karaoke is all about belting out lyrics, the opposite of a performer whose act depends entirely on staying quiet.
Things a mime uses at work.Air horn: An air horn can top 120 decibels, which would shatter the hush a mime depends on.
Things a mime uses at work.Trumpet: A trumpet is a loud brass instrument; a mime might pretend to play an imaginary one but wouldn't use a real horn.
Things a mime uses at work.Speech: Mime is speechless by definition; a spoken line breaks the illusion, which is why no one talks mid-act.
Things a mime uses at work.Bullhorn: A bullhorn is a handheld loudspeaker for crowds; a mime communicates with movement and has no use for one.
Things a mime uses at work.Shouting: Shouting is the opposite of a silent act, and a mime who speaks up has stepped out of character.
Things a mime uses at work.Singing: Singing would break the silence; acts that mix music and movement are mime's cousins, such as dance or musical theatre.
Things a mime uses at work.Kazoo: A kazoo hums your voice through a membrane, so it needs sound, and the silent mime is fine without one.
Things a mime uses at work.Telephone: A mime might pretend to use a phone, but a real one rings, and a ring would ruin the silent illusion.
Things a mime uses at work.Podcast: A podcast is audio-only, so it couldn't be more opposite to a visual, wordless act like mime.
Things a mime uses at work.Cymbals: Cymbals crash loudly in orchestras and marching bands, and in a mime's quiet act their noise would wreck everything.

Things a spy uses at work.Disguise: Spy agencies teach agents to change appearance with small tweaks like glasses, hats and posture, which work better than heavy makeup.
Things a spy uses at work.Code name: Operations carry code names so documents can mention them without revealing details; Operation Overlord, the D-Day invasion, is a famous one.
Things a spy uses at work.Invisible ink: Spies have used invisible ink for centuries; lemon juice and milk both work as simple versions, revealed by gentle heat.
Things a spy uses at work.Fake passport: Forged and doctored passports are a classic tradecraft tool, and modern biometric chips make them much harder to fake.
Things a spy uses at work.Hidden microphone: The Great Seal bug, hidden in a wooden plaque given to a US ambassador in Moscow, used no battery and went undetected for years.
Things a spy uses at work.Night vision goggles: Night vision devices amplify tiny amounts of light, and early versions were fielded by soldiers in World War II.
Things a spy uses at work.Cipher: The Enigma machine's cipher was broken by codebreakers including Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park, shortening the war.
Things a spy uses at work.Dead drop: A dead drop lets two spies pass items without ever meeting, by hiding them in a hollow tree or a loose brick.
Things a spy uses at work.Hidden camera: Tiny cameras were built for Cold War spies; the Minox became the classic subminiature camera of the era.
Things a spy uses at work.Safe house: A safe house is a secure place for hiding or meeting, and agencies often pick an ordinary flat or house that blends in.
Things a spy uses at work.Alias: An alias lets an agent move through the world unnoticed, and a good one comes with a backstory the agent must memorise.
Things a spy uses at work.Name tag: A name tag broadcasts your identity to everyone in the room, which is the last thing an undercover agent wants.
Things a spy uses at work.Neon sign: Neon signs are built to draw attention, so they suit a bar, not someone trying to stay unnoticed.
Things a spy uses at work.Billboard: A billboard is designed to be seen by thousands, whereas a spy needs to stay hidden.
Things a spy uses at work.Marching band: A marching band exists to be loud and seen, so a spy avoids anything like it, because secrecy needs quiet.
Things a spy uses at work.Fan club: Spies work in the shadows, so a fan club for an agent would blow cover; fan clubs are for celebrities.
Things a spy uses at work.Spotlight: A spotlight puts someone in plain view, the reverse of spy work, which depends on blending into the background.
Things a spy uses at work.Press release: Press releases announce things publicly, while spy agencies traditionally neither confirm nor deny their operations.
Things a spy uses at work.Autograph: Signing autographs means being recognised, which would end any covert career; it's a famous person's habit.
Things a spy uses at work.Livestream: A livestream shows the world what you're doing in real time, which is exactly what secret agents avoid.
Things a spy uses at work.Megaphone: Megaphones carry a voice across crowds, while an agent wants a whisper at most; police and protest leaders use them.
Things a spy uses at work.Loudspeaker: A loudspeaker makes sound big and public, whereas spies prefer devices that are small and silent.
Things a spy uses at work.Glitter cannon: A glitter cannon showers a crowd in sparkles, the loudest way to be noticed and a poor tool for hiding.
Things a spy uses at work.Selfie stick: A selfie stick puts your face into a photo shared online, which spells trouble for anyone with a secret identity.

Foods that are also computing terms.Cookie: Named after Unix 'magic cookies', it is a tiny file a website stores in your browser, invented in 1994 at Netscape by Lou Montulli.
Foods that are also computing terms.Spam: The email sense comes from a Monty Python sketch in which the canned meat is forced into every dish. Hormel's product dates to 1937.
Foods that are also computing terms.Java: The programming language was renamed after coffee, reportedly from the developers' favorite drink. The island of Java is where the beans grew.
Foods that are also computing terms.Chip: Tiny silicon chips hold billions of transistors. The name echoes a chip of stone or wood from the slice that was cut from a silicon wafer.
Foods that are also computing terms.Apple: The company took its name partly because Steve Jobs liked being listed ahead of Atari in the phone book, and the fruit is also its logo.
Foods that are also computing terms.BlackBerry: The phone maker's name was chosen because the keys looked like the fruit's tiny seeds. Its devices once dominated business email.
Foods that are also computing terms.Wafer: Chips are sliced from a thin disc of ultra-pure silicon crystal called a wafer, grown from a single crystal in a furnace.
Foods that are also computing terms.Kernel: The core of an operating system is its kernel, named for the seed at the heart of a nut. Linux is, technically, just a kernel.
Foods that are also computing terms.Hamburger: The hamburger menu, three stacked lines, was drawn in 1981 for the Xerox Star. Its resemblance to a burger came later.
Foods that are also computing terms.Breadcrumb: Navigation trails on websites borrow from Hansel and Gretel, who dropped crumbs to find their way home through the forest.
Foods that are also computing terms.Pizza: A trap: it's a tasty classic, but no computing term uses it. Bitcoin's first real-world purchase, in 2010, famously was two pizzas, though.
Foods that are also computing terms.Bagel: No computing meaning fits here, though a bagel's hole shape is the everyday example mathematicians use for a torus.
Foods that are also computing terms.Pancake: Not a computing term in common use. Mathematicians do study the 'pancake sorting' puzzle, though, where you flip a stack to order it.
Foods that are also computing terms.Noodle: Not a computing term. 'Spaghetti code', for tangled programs, is the related phrase, but it uses a different pasta word.
Foods that are also computing terms.Muffin: Not a computing term. English muffins are never baked in an oven but on a griddle, which is why they're flat and chewy.
Foods that are also computing terms.Lettuce: A computing non-starter. In 2022 a supermarket lettuce famously outlasted British prime minister Liz Truss in a livestreamed contest.
Foods that are also computing terms.Carrot: No computing sense, but the caret symbol (^) is often misnamed 'carrot' because the two sound alike.
Foods that are also computing terms.Broccoli: Not a computing term. Broccoli was bred in Italy from wild cabbage and has been eaten since Roman times.
Foods that are also computing terms.Taco: Not a computing term, although 'Taco Tuesday' is a US trademark claim that Taco John's long defended before giving it up in 2023.
Foods that are also computing terms.Burrito: No computing meaning. The word means 'little donkey' in Spanish, and the roll-up-your-food style became a San Francisco specialty.
Foods that are also computing terms.Sushi: No computing meaning. The word actually refers to the vinegared rice, not the raw fish, which is sashimi when served alone.
Foods that are also computing terms.Lasagna: Not a computing word, though 'lasagna code' is a joke term for layers of software so neatly stacked that changing one layer is hard.
Foods that are also computing terms.Cheese: Not a computing term. Swiss Emmental's holes are formed by gas bubbles released by bacteria during ripening.
Foods that are also computing terms.Soup: Not a computing term, though 'alphabet soup' is what techies call a bewildering pile of acronyms like HTTP, FTP and SMTP.

Horses in literature.Black Beauty: Black Beauty is Anna Sewell's 1877 horse narrator, and the book changed how Victorians treated horses.
Horses in literature.Shadowfax: Shadowfax is the lord of horses who carries Gandalf, so swift that no one else could ride him.
Horses in literature.Rocinante: Rocinante is Don Quixote's thin old horse, with a name that a lordly knight chose after much thought.
Horses in literature.Boxer: Boxer is the loyal cart-horse in Animal Farm, whose motto is I will work harder, and who is sent to the knacker.
Horses in literature.Joey: Joey is the horse in Michael Morpurgo's War Horse, who ends up on the Western Front in World War I.
Horses in literature.Bree: Bree is a talking horse in C. S. Lewis's The Horse and His Boy; the name is also a Middle-earth town.
Horses in literature.Ginger: Ginger is Black Beauty's chestnut friend, a spirited mare worn down by cruel treatment.
Horses in literature.Merrylegs: Merrylegs is the plump, good-natured pony in Black Beauty who carries the children.
Horses in literature.Bill the Pony: Bill the Pony is the sad but sturdy pack animal that carries Fellowship supplies through Moria.
Horses in literature.Misty: Misty is the Chincoteague pony in Marguerite Henry's 1947 Misty of Chincoteague, a real island's story.
Horses in literature.Flicka: Flicka is the wild mustang in Mary O'Hara's My Friend Flicka, whose name is Swedish for girl.
Horses in literature.Buckbeak: Buckbeak is a hippogriff, half horse and half eagle, so he's not a pure horse.
Horses in literature.Toto: Toto is a dog, Dorothy's terrier in The Wizard of Oz, so he doesn't belong in a horse group.
Horses in literature.Eeyore: Eeyore is the gloomy donkey in Winnie-the-Pooh, who loses his tail; a donkey isn't a horse.
Horses in literature.Benjamin: Benjamin is the cynical donkey in Animal Farm, so he's not a horse, unlike Boxer.
Horses in literature.Falkor: Falkor is the luckdragon in The NeverEnding Story, who looks like a flying dog, not a horse.
Horses in literature.Hedwig: Hedwig is Harry's snowy owl, a birthday present from Hagrid, so she's a bird, not a horse.
Horses in literature.Aslan: Aslan is the lion of Narnia, not a horse, though the talking horse Bree is another Narnian.
Horses in literature.Fawkes: Fawkes is Dumbledore's phoenix, who bursts into flame and is reborn, so not a horse.
Horses in literature.Lassie: Lassie is a collie from Eric Knight's 1940 story, famous for trekking home across Britain, and not a horse.
Horses in literature.Bambi: Bambi is a young deer in Felix Salten's 1923 novel, which Disney adapted in 1942, not a horse.
Horses in literature.Babe: Babe is the pig who herds sheep in Dick King-Smith's The Sheep-Pig, so he's not a horse.
Horses in literature.Smaug: Smaug is the golden-red dragon of The Hobbit, who sleeps on a hoard of treasure, so he's no horse.
Horses in literature.Moby Dick: Moby Dick is the white whale that Captain Ahab hunts in Melville's novel, so not a horse.

Female artists.Frida Kahlo: She painted self-portraits in about a third of her works, many made in bed while recovering from a bus accident at eighteen.
Female artists.Georgia O'Keeffe: Her giant flowers and desert bones made her a pioneer of American modernism, and she settled in New Mexico, near Abiquiu.
Female artists.Mary Cassatt: An American in Paris who exhibited with the Impressionists at Degas's invitation. She is famed for intimate scenes of mothers and children.
Female artists.Berthe Morisot: The first woman to join the Impressionists, she exhibited at their 1874 debut, and she married Manet's brother Eugene.
Female artists.Yayoi Kusama: She is famed for polka dots and mirrored Infinity Rooms, and has lived by choice in a Tokyo psychiatric hospital since 1977.
Female artists.Louise Bourgeois: Her nine-meter spider sculpture, Maman, honors her mother, a tapestry restorer. Casts stand around the world.
Female artists.Barbara Hepworth: British sculptor of pierced abstract forms. Her bronze Single Form stands outside the UN in New York.
Female artists.Tamara de Lempicka: Polish-born Art Deco portraitist whose glossy, metallic style defined the Jazz Age. Madonna is a well-known collector.
Female artists.Bridget Riley: A pioneer of Op Art whose black-and-white wave patterns from the 1960s can make viewers feel dizzy.
Female artists.Hilma af Klint: This Swedish artist made abstract paintings from 1906, before Kandinsky, and asked that they stay hidden for twenty years after her death.
Female artists.Cindy Sherman: She photographs herself in invented roles, as in her Untitled Film Stills, and one photograph sold for about $3.9 million in 2011.
Female artists.Lee Krasner: An Abstract Expressionist, she was married to Jackson Pollock and became a major painter in her own right after his 1956 death.
Female artists.Rosa Bonheur: Her 1853 painting The Horse Fair made her France's best-known woman painter, and she obtained police permission to wear trousers.
Female artists.Diego Rivera: Mexican muralist and Kahlo's husband. He was a man and the more famous of the pair in his day, so he doesn't fit.
Female artists.Jackson Pollock: The drip painter, a man, who was married to Lee Krasner. She belongs on the list, but he doesn't, however famous he was.
Female artists.Alfred Stieglitz: The photographer who championed and married Georgia O'Keeffe. He's a man and was no artist of her list.
Female artists.Edgar Degas: He encouraged Mary Cassatt to join the Impressionists, but he's a man, so he's no match for this category.
Female artists.Pablo Picasso: A man, though his lover Dora Maar, a painter and photographer, belongs on a women artists list.
Female artists.Mark Rothko: He painted soft-edged blocks of color. A male Abstract Expressionist, so he's not among the women.
Female artists.Henri Matisse: A man who founded Fauvism and, near the end of his life, made cut-paper art from his bed, so he's no fit here.
Female artists.Joan Miró: Despite "Joan" being a woman's name in English, he was a Catalan man, famous for playful, dreamlike abstraction.
Female artists.Man Ray: The American photographer. His muse and partner Lee Miller was herself a great photographer, but he is the man.
Female artists.Francis Bacon: An Irish-born British painter of screaming figures, no relation to the philosopher of the same name.
Female artists.Lucian Freud: Sigmund Freud's grandson, a man, who painted thick, unflinching nudes and portraits, so he's not a female artist.

Plays by American playwrights.The Crucible: Miller wrote it in 1953 about the Salem witch trials, as an allegory for the McCarthy-era hunt for communists.
Plays by American playwrights.Death of a Salesman: It won the 1949 Pulitzer Prize, and Miller reportedly wrote much of it in about six weeks.
Plays by American playwrights.Our Town: Thornton Wilder's 1938 play uses a nearly bare stage and a narrator, still staged in schools.
Plays by American playwrights.The Glass Menagerie: Tennessee Williams's 1944 memory play centers on Laura and her glass unicorn, based partly on his own sister.
Plays by American playwrights.Fences: August Wilson's 1983 play, part of his ten-play Century Cycle, won the 1987 Pulitzer Prize.
Plays by American playwrights.Angels in America: Tony Kushner's two-part epic about AIDS in the 1980s won the 1993 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
Plays by American playwrights.A Raisin in the Sun: The first play by a Black woman on Broadway, 1959. The title comes from a Langston Hughes poem.
Plays by American playwrights.Glengarry Glen Ross: David Mamet's 1983 play about real estate salesmen. The "coffee is for closers" speech was written for the 1992 film.
Plays by American playwrights.The Iceman Cometh: Eugene O'Neill's 1939 play is set in a dingy bar and runs about four hours, and he is the only American playwright to win the Nobel Prize.
Plays by American playwrights.All My Sons: Miller's first Broadway hit, in 1947, about a factory that shipped defective airplane parts in wartime.
Plays by American playwrights.The Odd Couple: Neil Simon's 1965 play, the source of a film and TV show about the tidy Felix and slovenly Oscar.
Plays by American playwrights.Doubt: John Patrick Shanley's 2004 Pulitzer winner about a nun's suspicions of a priest, with its subtitle "A Parable".
Plays by American playwrights.Pygmalion: George Bernard Shaw was Irish and wrote it in 1913, and it became the musical My Fair Lady.
Plays by American playwrights.Waiting for Godot: Samuel Beckett was Irish and wrote it first in French, and it premiered in Paris in 1953, not America.
Plays by American playwrights.Look Back in Anger: John Osborne's 1956 English play launched the "angry young men" and was set in a cramped Midlands flat.
Plays by American playwrights.Equus: Peter Shaffer's 1973 English play about a boy who blinds horses, and a psychiatrist who treats him.
Plays by American playwrights.The History Boys: Alan Bennett's 2004 play was staged by the National Theatre in London, so it's very British.
Plays by American playwrights.Private Lives: Noël Coward, an Englishman, wrote it in 1930, and it's a comedy of divorced lovers who meet again.
Plays by American playwrights.Blithe Spirit: Coward's 1941 comedy ran 1,997 performances in London, a record for a non-musical at the time.
Plays by American playwrights.Hedda Gabler: Henrik Ibsen was Norwegian, and this play was first staged in 1891, so no American author.
Plays by American playwrights.The Seagull: Chekhov, a Russian, saw it fail at its 1896 premiere, then triumph in 1898 in Moscow, so not American.
Plays by American playwrights.An Inspector Calls: J. B. Priestley, an Englishman, set it in 1912, though it premiered in Moscow in 1945, not in America.
Plays by American playwrights.The Mousetrap: Agatha Christie's English play has run in London since 1952, the longest run in the world.
Plays by American playwrights.Noises Off: Michael Frayn, an Englishman, wrote this farce about a troupe putting on a play, as seen from backstage.

Shiny things.Mirror: Mirrors reflect nearly all light in an orderly way, unlike matte surfaces that scatter it, and the first ones were polished obsidian.
Shiny things.Diamond: A diamond's sparkle comes from its very high refractive index, which bends light and traps it before sending it back out the top.
Shiny things.Gold bar: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube roughly 21 meters on a side, and gold's luster never tarnishes since it hardly reacts with air.
Shiny things.Disco ball: Mirrored balls scatter spotlights into hundreds of beams, and they rose to fame in discos in the 1970s, though invented earlier.
Shiny things.Tinfoil: Kitchen foil is nowadays made of aluminum, not tin, and it has a shiny side and a dull side only because of how it is rolled.
Shiny things.Sequins: Sequins are small reflective discs sewn onto clothes, and their name comes from the Venetian gold coin called the zecchino.
Shiny things.Glitter: Glitter is tiny pieces of reflective plastic or metal film, and its pieces are so small and numerous that they get everywhere and are hard to clean up.
Shiny things.Chrome bumper: Chrome plating is a thin layer of chromium over steel, and chrome bumpers were a signature of 1950s American cars.
Shiny things.Tinsel: Tinsel was first made of real silver strips in 1600s Germany, which tarnished, before cheaper materials replaced it.
Shiny things.New penny: A fresh copper penny shines since its surface is bare copper, and it dulls to brown as it oxidizes with air and handling.
Shiny things.Pearl: Pearls grow inside oysters when a mollusk coats an irritant in layers of nacre, and the layers give a pearl its lustre.
Shiny things.Patent leather: Leather coated in lacquer gets a glassy shine, and it was developed in the 1800s, with Seth Boyden making the first American version.
Shiny things.Chalk: Chalk is a soft limestone made from tiny sea creatures' shells, with a dull powdery surface that doesn't reflect light.
Shiny things.Cardboard: Cardboard is dull because paper fibers scatter light in every direction, so no clear reflection is possible.
Shiny things.Brick: Brick is a rough, matte fired clay, and it scatters light, not reflecting it like a polished surface would.
Shiny things.Felt: Felt is a mat of tangled fibers, and its fuzzy surface scatters light so completely that it looks soft and dull.
Shiny things.Wool: Wool fibers have tiny scales, which scatter light, giving a soft matte appearance rather than a gleam.
Shiny things.Sandpaper: Sandpaper's rough grit scatters light and makes a surface dull, and its job is to scratch a surface into smoothness.
Shiny things.Cotton ball: A cotton ball is mostly air and soft white fiber, and every strand scatters light, so it has no gleam.
Shiny things.Flour: Flour is a fine powder that scatters light, so it looks bright white without any glossiness.
Shiny things.Charcoal: Charcoal is porous carbon that absorbs most light, which is why it appears a deep, flat black.
Shiny things.Concrete: Concrete has a rough, gritty surface made of cement and stone, so it reflects light diffusely, with no shine.
Shiny things.Tree bark: Bark's rough texture helps shield a tree, and it is one of the most reliably matte textures in nature.
Shiny things.Paper bag: A paper bag has a matte, fibrous finish and is made of kraft paper, a German word for strength.

Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Rice: Rice is the staple food for about half the world's population, and it contains no gluten.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Corn: Corn's main protein is zein, not gluten, so plain corn is safe for gluten-free diets.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Potato: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes around 8,000 years ago and are naturally gluten-free.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Quinoa: Quinoa is a seed, not a grain, and the Incas called it the 'mother grain'.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Buckwheat: Despite the name, buckwheat isn't related to wheat; it's a relative of rhubarb.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Rice noodles: Rice noodles, found in pho and pad thai, are made from rice flour and water, with no gluten.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Polenta: Polenta is boiled cornmeal, and cornmeal contains no gluten.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Tapioca: Tapioca comes from the cassava root, and it forms the chewy pearls in bubble tea.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Millet: Millet is one of the oldest cultivated grains and has been farmed in Asia and Africa for thousands of years.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Popcorn: Plain popcorn is a gluten-free whole grain, though flavored versions may contain additives.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Sorghum: Sorghum originated in Africa, and is among the most important cereals in the world.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.White bread: Gluten is the protein network in wheat dough that traps gas so that white bread rises.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Pasta: Pasta is traditionally durum wheat, which is gluten-rich and gives it firmness.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Couscous: Couscous is made from wheat semolina, so it contains gluten despite its grainy look.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Barley: Barley contains hordein, a gluten-type protein, which is why malted barley beer isn't safe.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Rye: Rye contains a gluten protein called secalin, so rye bread isn't gluten-free.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Bulgur: Bulgur is cracked wheat, so it contains gluten, even though it looks like a grain of rice.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Spelt: Spelt is an ancient wheat species, so it contains gluten, even if it's often marketed as healthier.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Seitan: Seitan is basically pure wheat gluten, which earns it the nickname 'wheat meat'.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Croissant: Croissants rely on wheat gluten to trap steam from the butter layers and puff up.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Beer: Most beer is brewed with barley malt, which has gluten, though gluten-removed versions exist.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Soy sauce: Traditional soy sauce is brewed with wheat, a surprise for many; tamari is often wheat-free.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Pretzel: Pretzels are made from wheat flour, so the gluten gives them their chew.
Foods that are naturally gluten-free.Semolina: Semolina is coarsely ground durum wheat, the main ingredient of pasta.

Things lighter than a paperclip.Down feather: Down feathers trap air and weigh almost nothing, which is why a duvet can be warm yet very light.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Snowflake: A snowflake weighs about a milligram, and each one has six sides because of how water molecules lock together.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Grain of rice: A single grain of rice weighs about 20 milligrams, roughly a fortieth of a paperclip.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Ant: An ant weighs only a few milligrams but can carry loads many times its own body weight.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Postage stamp: A stamp weighs a small fraction of a gram, well under a paperclip, and philately is one of the oldest hobbies.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Raindrop: A raindrop is only a few milligrams, and a falling one is round rather than teardrop-shaped.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Sesame seed: A sesame seed weighs about three milligrams, and the 'open sesame' phrase is thought to refer to its popping pods.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Eyelash: An eyelash weighs a tiny fraction of a milligram, and each lasts about two months before it is replaced.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Dandelion seed: A dandelion seed weighs well under a milligram, and its parachute can carry it for kilometers on the breeze.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Mosquito: A mosquito weighs only a couple of milligrams, and it is the female that bites.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Strand of hair: A single hair weighs a tiny fraction of a milligram and can support a surprising weight before it snaps.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Flea: A flea weighs about a milligram and can leap over 100 times its own body length.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Hummingbird: A hummingbird weighs a few grams, heavier than a paperclip, and the smallest, the bee hummingbird, is about two grams.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Penny: A US penny weighs 2.5 grams, which is much heavier than a paperclip.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Sugar cube: A sugar cube is about four grams, which is several times a paperclip.
Things lighter than a paperclip.AA battery: An AA battery weighs around 23 grams, far more than a paperclip, which is under a gram.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Golf ball: A golf ball can weigh no more than 45.93 grams under the rules, so it is much heavier than a paperclip.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Pencil: A standard pencil weighs several grams, so it is heavier than a paperclip, which weighs about a gram.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Mouse: A house mouse weighs around 20 grams, many times more than a paperclip.
Things lighter than a paperclip.Egg: A hen's egg weighs around 50 grams, so it is far heavier than a paperclip.

Crispy outside and soft inside.Churro: Churros fry up crunchy and ridged with a doughy center, and in Spain they're often dunked in thick hot chocolate.

Crispy outside and soft inside.Baguette: A baguette's crackly crust comes from steam in the oven, and the soft crumb inside has big holes.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Arancini: Arancini are Sicilian rice balls, and the name means little oranges for their golden color.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Croquette: Croquette comes from the French for crunch, and the creamy filling inside is often a thick potato or béchamel.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Toasted marshmallow: Toasting browns the outside through caramelization while the inside turns gooey, which is why s'mores work.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Macaron: A macaron has a thin crisp shell and a chewy middle, and it's a French meringue-based cookie, not a coconut macaroon.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Hush puppy: A fried cornmeal ball that's crunchy on the outside and fluffy within, a Southern companion to fried fish.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Candy apple: A hard sugar shell covers the apple, and it cracks with the first bite to reveal the juicy fruit.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Pudding: Pudding is soft all the way through, with no crisp shell.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Banana: A banana is soft all the way, and its peel is bendable, with no crispy layer.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Mashed potatoes: Mashed potatoes are soft throughout, with no crisp contrast.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Jell-O: Jell-O is wobbly throughout and has no crispy side.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Yogurt: Yogurt is creamy throughout, and has no crisp part.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Cracker: Crackers are crisp all the way through, and the name comes from the cracking sound they make.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Hard pretzel: Hard pretzels are crunchy all through, unlike soft pretzels, which are chewy.

Crispy outside and soft inside.Ice cream: Ice cream is smooth all through, though dipped cones add a crisp shell.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Applesauce: Applesauce is a soft puree throughout, with no crisp part.
Crispy outside and soft inside.Rice cake: Puffed rice cakes are crunchy and airy all through, and Korean tteok are chewy.

Things you'd see at a train station.Platform: The longest railway platform in the world, at Hubballi in India, is about 1.5 km long.
Things you'd see at a train station.Ticket machine: Self-service ticket machines now sell most tickets, and Edmondson's cardboard tickets of the 1840s used to be stamped by hand.
Things you'd see at a train station.Timetable: Railways created standard time zones so that timetables worked, and before them each town kept its own local time.
Things you'd see at a train station.Departure board: The classic flapping split-flap boards made a distinctive clacking sound, and are largely replaced by LED screens.
Things you'd see at a train station.Turnstile: Turnstiles at stations control entry, and the first was an 1890s invention to count passengers.
Things you'd see at a train station.Waiting room: Waiting rooms were once divided into first, second and third class, and many still keep their old fireplaces.
Things you'd see at a train station.Footbridge: Footbridges let passengers cross the tracks safely, and the Victorian lattice ones are now icons.
Things you'd see at a train station.Signal: Railway signals evolved from semaphore arms in the 1840s, and today colored lights show whether the line ahead is clear.
Things you'd see at a train station.Rails: Standard gauge, 4 feet 8.5 inches, is used in most countries, and it traces back to early English tramways.
Things you'd see at a train station.Station clock: Swiss railway clocks, designed in 1944, have a red second hand shaped like a station guard's signal disc that pauses at the top of the minute.
Things you'd see at a train station.Conductor: A train conductor checks tickets, and the term also names the person who leads an orchestra.
Things you'd see at a train station.Locomotive: A railway engine, and the word comes from Latin 'loco' (from a place) and 'motivus' (causing motion).
Things you'd see at a train station.Runway: An airport strip, and no train station needs one.
Things you'd see at a train station.Jet bridge: An airport tool for boarding planes, not for trains.
Things you'd see at a train station.Baggage carousel: The luggage belt at airports, not at train stations, which normally keep bags with you.
Things you'd see at a train station.Control tower: Air traffic controllers sit in these at airports, not at stations.
Things you'd see at a train station.Windsock: An airfield indicator of wind direction, not seen at train stations.
Things you'd see at a train station.Hangar: An aircraft shed, named from a French word for a shed, and found at airfields, never at stations, where trains use sheds called depots.
Things you'd see at a train station.Gangplank: A ship's boarding ramp, so it belongs at a dock; train passengers just step up from the platform, with no plank in sight.
Things you'd see at a train station.Lighthouse: A beacon on the coast, so not at train stations.
Things you'd see at a train station.Anchor: Boats use anchors, and trains rely on brakes.
Things you'd see at a train station.Pit lane: A racetrack pit area for car servicing, so not at a station.
Things you'd see at a train station.Taxiway: Airport roads for aircraft, so not at a train station.
Things you'd see at a train station.Hot air balloon: Balloons fly from fields, not stations, though a few railway parks do offer rides.

Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Pall Mall: A magenta property whose name is said to come from a French game similar to croquet; it's pronounced 'pell mell'.

Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Leicester Square: A yellow property whose name is pronounced 'Lester', and it's a famous London site for film premieres.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Euston Road: This light blue property is a busy road that passes some of London's main railway stations.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Bow Street: The orange property is the street where Britain's first police force, the Bow Street Runners, was based.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Baker Street: Sherlock Holmes's fictional address, 221B, is here, but the street isn't a Monopoly space.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Abbey Road: The Beatles' famous album cover crossing isn't on the Monopoly board, even though London is.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Downing Street: The home of the prime minister at Number 10 isn't a Monopoly property.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Carnaby Street: The 1960s fashion street in Soho isn't on the board, though it's one of London's best known.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Portobello Road: The famed Notting Hill market street isn't a Monopoly space.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Covent Garden: This former market and theater district isn't on the UK board, but it's a London landmark.
Spaces on the UK Monopoly board.Notting Hill: The west London neighborhood, made famous by a 1999 film, isn't a Monopoly property.

Animals used for transport.Horse: Horses were the main way of long-distance travel for thousands of years; the pony express riders changed horses every 10-15 miles.
Animals used for transport.Camel: A dromedary can carry about 200 kg and go several days without water, which made caravans possible across the Sahara.
Animals used for transport.Donkey: Donkeys have carried goods since around 4000 BC and are surefooted on steep mountain trails where horses struggle.
Animals used for transport.Elephant: Asian elephants have long been used to haul logs and carry people, and a trained one can carry loads of about 450 kg.
Animals used for transport.Mule: A mule is the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse; it is prized for strength and surefootedness, and is almost always sterile.
Animals used for transport.Ox: Oxen pulled the covered wagons of the American pioneers, and they were often preferred to horses for their strength and stamina.
Animals used for transport.Yak: Yaks carry heavy loads across the Himalayas at altitudes where other animals struggle, thanks to their huge lungs.
Animals used for transport.Llama: Llamas were the pack animals of the Andes, able to carry about a quarter of their body weight, and they were used by the Inca.
Animals used for transport.Reindeer: Sami and other Arctic herders have long used reindeer to pull sleds, and they remain a working transport animal today.
Animals used for transport.Husky: Sled dogs like huskies were used for delivering the 1925 serum run to Nome, Alaska, which inspired the Iditarod race.
Animals used for transport.Water buffalo: Water buffalo pull carts and plows across Asia, and are well suited to wet, muddy rice paddies.
Animals used for transport.Giraffe: A trap: giraffes are tall and strong, but their build and temperament, and a spine unsuited to a rider, rule out regular transport.
Animals used for transport.Hippo: Hippos are aggressive and kill more people in Africa than lions do, so nobody has ever managed to domesticate them.
Animals used for transport.Kangaroo: Kangaroos can't be ridden or harnessed; they hop at up to 70 km/h but resist domestication.
Animals used for transport.Cheetah: Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, but they are too light to carry a rider and cannot be domesticated for transport.
Animals used for transport.Panda: Giant pandas eat bamboo for most of the day and are not used for transport, in spite of being one of the best-loved bears.
Animals used for transport.Rhino: Rhinos are heavy and powerful, but they are not tame, and no culture has used them as a regular transport animal.
Animals used for transport.Gorilla: Gorillas are gentle but strong and wild, and humans have never used them to carry loads or people.
Animals used for transport.Sloth: Sloths move so slowly, around 0.25 km/h on the ground, that algae can grow on their fur. Hardly a ride.
Animals used for transport.Koala: Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day and are not used for transport; they're marsupials, not bears.
Animals used for transport.Bear: Bears have been trained for circuses, but they are too unpredictable and dangerous to be used for regular transport.
Animals used for transport.Lion: Lions are apex predators, not working animals, and no society has used them to carry people or goods.
Animals used for transport.Penguin: Penguins swim superbly but cannot carry anything bigger than themselves, and most species live only in the southern hemisphere.
Animals used for transport.Flamingo: Flamingos get their pink from the carotenoids in their food, and they are far too light to carry a person.
